result: In wild-type mice with non-specific DREADD expression and ChAT-Cre mice with targeted phrenic motoneuron DREADD expression, J60 administration produced sustained bilateral increases in diaphragm EMG output (AUC, peak-to-peak amplitude, and tonic activity) without substantially changing respiratory rate in wild-type mice, though respiratory rate decreased in ChAT-Cre mice.
evaluation: Claims C2-C3 establish the experimental design with appropriate controls (non-specific vs. targeted expression). Claims C18-C28 provide consistent statistical evidence (p<0.05 for most measures) showing J60-induced increases in diaphragm EMG parameters in both mouse strains. The data demonstrate bilateral responses in most animals with appropriate statistical testing (one-way RM ANOVA). The results are internally consistent and supported by referenced figures.

result: ChAT-Cre mice showed significantly greater right hemidiaphragm responses to J60 compared to wild-type mice across all EMG measures (AUC, peak-to-peak amplitude, tonic activity), while left hemidiaphragm responses and respiratory rate were similar between groups.
evaluation: Claims C29-C31 provide direct statistical comparisons between wild-type and ChAT-Cre mice with appropriate p-values. The finding that targeted expression (ChAT-Cre) produces greater responses than non-specific expression (wild-type) on the right side is consistent with the histological data showing more prevalent right-sided expression in ChAT-Cre mice (C52). Statistical tests are appropriate (paired t-tests) and results are referenced to Figure 3.

result: Five of eleven wild-type mice did not survive the 90-minute recording duration, while all ChAT-Cre mice survived, though this difference was not statistically significant (p=0.069).
evaluation: Claims C32-C34 report survival data with appropriate statistical testing (Chi-square). However, the p-value of 0.069 is marginally non-significant, and the authors acknowledge uncertainty about whether mortality was related to DREADD activation or prolonged anesthesia. The small sample size (n=11 wild-type, n=9 ChAT-Cre) limits statistical power to detect differences. This raises safety concerns that require further investigation.

result: In control experiments with animals not expressing hM3D(Gq), J60 administration had no effect on diaphragm EMG burst amplitude in either hemidiaphragm.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 provide appropriate negative control data showing J60 has no effect without DREADD expression (p>0.05 for all comparisons). This validates the specificity of the DREADD-ligand system. The control experiments included both mice and rats (n=5 total), and statistical tests (one-way RM ANOVA and paired t-tests) were appropriate. Results are referenced to Figure 4.

result: In ChAT-Cre rats, J60 administration increased inspiratory tidal volume (p=0.037) without affecting respiratory rate (p=0.582), while minute ventilation showed a non-significant trend toward increase (p=0.194).
evaluation: Claims C37-C40 demonstrate functional respiratory outcomes in awake, spontaneously breathing rats using whole-body plethysmography. The significant increase in tidal volume (C38) with stable respiratory rate (C39) indicates effective diaphragm activation. The non-significant minute ventilation increase (C40) is consistent with the modest tidal volume increase and stable rate. Statistical testing (two-way RM ANOVA) is appropriate, and results are referenced to Figure 5. Sample size (n=9 rats) is adequate.

result: In anesthetized ChAT-Cre rats, J60 caused rapid, sustained (>100 min), bilateral increases in phrenic nerve burst amplitude (>200% baseline, p<0.001) and tonic activity (p<0.001), with decreased blood pressure (p<0.001) but no changes in heart rate (p=0.587) or respiratory rate (p=0.282).
evaluation: Claims C41-C49 provide direct phrenic nerve recordings under controlled conditions (urethane anesthesia, controlled blood gases). The >200% increase in phrenic output (C42) is substantial and highly significant. The sustained duration (C43) and bilateral nature of the response support the functional efficacy. The blood pressure decrease (C47-C49) is a notable side effect that requires consideration for clinical translation. Statistical testing is appropriate (one-way RM ANOVA), and results are referenced to Figure 6. The lack of relationship between time post-injection and response (C41) suggests stable DREADD expression.

result: Histological analysis revealed mCherry expression in the mid-cervical spinal cord of all included animals, with wild-type mice showing relatively homogenous expression throughout the gray matter, while ChAT-Cre mice and rats showed expression predominantly in the ventral horns with greater prevalence on the right side in ChAT-Cre mice.
evaluation: Claims C50-C53 provide histological validation of DREADD expression patterns. The qualitative assessment is appropriate given the study design. The correlation between expression patterns and physiological responses (e.g., greater right-sided expression in ChAT-Cre mice correlating with greater right hemidiaphragm responses) supports the validity of the findings. The exclusion of one ChAT-Cre mouse without expression (C50) was appropriate based on a priori criteria. Results are referenced to Figures 7 and 8.

result: The authors conclude that targeting mid-cervical spinal DREADD expression to phrenic motoneurons enables sustained increases in phrenic motor output and tidal volume, and that DREADDs should be directed exclusively to phrenic motoneurons rather than non-specifically expressed.
evaluation: Claims C54, C70, and C71 represent the main conclusions. These are well-supported by the experimental data showing: (1) sustained increases in diaphragm EMG, phrenic nerve output, and tidal volume across multiple experimental paradigms; (2) greater and more consistent responses in ChAT-Cre animals with targeted expression compared to wild-type animals with non-specific expression; and (3) appropriate control experiments demonstrating specificity. The recommendation for exclusive targeting (C71) is justified by the comparative data and potential safety concerns in wild-type mice.

result: The authors acknowledge variability in laterality of mCherry expression and physiological responses, attributing this to subtle variations in surgical positioning or needle placement, and recommend improving AAV delivery methods for more precise targeting.
evaluation: Claims C67 and C72 appropriately acknowledge methodological limitations. The observed variability in expression patterns (documented in C50-C53) and corresponding physiological responses (C22, C28) supports this interpretation. The recommendation for improved delivery methods (C72) is reasonable given the observed variability. This represents appropriate scientific self-critique and suggests directions for future work.

result: The authors propose mechanistic explanations for DREADD effects, including lowering activation thresholds of phrenic motoneurons, direct induction of action potentials, and activation of propriospinal networks, while noting that inhibitory feedback mechanisms (vagal, blood gas-related) may constrain responses in spontaneously breathing animals compared to controlled nerve recordings.
evaluation: Claims C57-C66 provide mechanistic interpretations based on established respiratory physiology (C56, C62, C63) and the experimental data. The observation that phrenic nerve responses (~250% baseline, C65) were greater than diaphragm EMG responses in spontaneously breathing animals (~100% baseline, C65) supports the inference that feedback mechanisms constrain responses (C66). The proposed mechanisms (C57-C60) are plausible given DREADD function and are consistent with the observed tonic discharge (C59). These interpretations appropriately integrate prior knowledge with current findings.

result: Pilot experiments using intrapleural and intramuscular diaphragm injections with AAV9 vectors did not produce evidence of phrenic motoneuron transduction, leading the authors to predict that different AAV serotypes or retrograde viruses could optimize targeting.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 report negative pilot data that informed the final experimental design. The failure of alternative delivery methods (C81) justifies the use of direct intraspinal injection. The prediction about alternative serotypes (C82) is reasonable and supported by citation to prior work on AAV retro. This represents appropriate reporting of negative results and methodological development.

result: The authors speculate that further development of this technology may enable clinical applications for conditions with impaired diaphragm activation, such as incomplete cervical spinal cord injury.
evaluation: Claims C55, C73, and C74 are explicitly speculative statements about potential clinical applications. While the proof-of-concept data support the feasibility of DREADD-mediated phrenic activation, substantial additional work would be required for clinical translation, including: addressing the blood pressure decrease observed in rats (C47-C49), resolving the potential safety concerns in wild-type mice (C32-C34), improving targeting precision (C67, C72), and demonstrating efficacy in disease models. These are appropriate forward-looking statements but remain speculative.

result: The introduction establishes that impaired respiratory motor output contributes to morbidity in neurological conditions, that DREADDs are engineered receptors responsive to selective ligands, that prior work has used DREADDs to activate hypoglossal motoneurons, and that non-specific cervical spinal activation can increase diaphragm output.
evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C17 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims establish the rationale for the study by documenting: (1) the clinical problem (C1, C8, C9); (2) the DREADD technology (C10); (3) prior applications to respiratory motoneurons (C11-C13); (4) relevant anatomy (C14); and (5) prior work on cervical spinal stimulation (C15-C17). The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with established understanding.

result: The authors argue that mCherry expression was clearly in the expected location of phrenic motoneurons based on prior anatomical descriptions, and that the robust phrenic output increase provides evidence of effective targeting.
evaluation: Claims C68-C69 address the limitation that retrograde labeling was not used to definitively confirm phrenic motoneuron targeting. The argument is reasonable given: (1) well-established anatomical descriptions of the phrenic motor nucleus (cited in C68); (2) histological evidence showing ventral horn expression in the appropriate location (C50-C53, Figure 7); and (3) functional evidence of robust phrenic output increases (C42, C69). While retrograde labeling would have been more definitive, the convergent evidence supports the conclusion.

result: The discussion contextualizes the work within prior literature on viral vector delivery to phrenic motoneurons, DREADD applications to motoneurons, and hypoglossal DREADD studies, positioning this as the first application of DREADD technology to phrenic motoneurons.
evaluation: Claims C75-C90 provide appropriate literature context with citations. The claim of novelty (C90) appears justified given the cited literature showing prior DREADD work focused on hypoglossal motoneurons (C87-C89) and limited applications to spinal motoneurons (C84-C86). The discussion of alternative delivery methods (C75-C80) appropriately acknowledges other approaches and explains methodological choices. These claims provide appropriate scholarly context.
